Female Scalebelly eelpout attain a maximum total length of 26 cm [Li = 26 cm], a value derived from extensive field sampling across the Bering Sea slope. This ultimate size represents a substantial investment in somatic growth before reproductive allocation begins. In contrast, total length at puberty for females is reached at 14 cm [Lp = 14 cm], indicating that the onset of gonadal maturation occurs relatively early in the lifespan, when individuals have achieved slightly more than half of their asymptotic length. The length-weight relationship for this species suggests that a female of 14 cm would correspond to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 14 g [Wwp = approximately 14 g]. This transition to reproductive capability at a moderate body size is consistent with a life-history strategy that favors early breeding in a cold, resource-limited environment. Such early maturation may be advantageous given the protracted developmental schedules imposed by persistently low ambient temperatures in the deep demersal habitats this zoarcid occupies.

Newly hatched larvae of Lycodes squamiventer emerge from demersal eggs following an incubation period that yields a very small neonate. The wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.0224 g [Wwb = 0.0224 g], a mass derived from the predicted egg diameter of 3.5 millimeters. This exceedingly low birth mass, typical of marine teleosts with pelagic larval phases, necessitates a period of intense yolk-sac absorption before the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larva depends entirely on endogenous reserves during the first days post-hatching, and the timing of first feeding is critical for survival. The small size at hatching contrasts sharply with the ultimate wet weight of 40 g [Wwi = 40 g] attained by asymptotic females, illustrating the enormous scope for post-hatching growth. This nearly 1800-fold increase in body mass from birth to adulthood underscores the importance of high feeding rates during the juvenile and sub-adult stages in these cold waters.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable temperature of 0.9 °C [T = 0.9 °C], females exhibit a maximum reproductive output of approximately 55 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 55 eggs per year], a value calculated from the ratio of clutch size to spawning interval. This low annual fecundity is typical of high-latitude zoarcids, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by near-freezing waters. The low temperature slows metabolic processes, including vitellogenesis and oocyte maturation, thereby limiting the frequency with which females can produce viable clutches. Field observations corroborate these laboratory findings, suggesting that reproductive events are spaced widely throughout the year, with most spawning activity concentrated during the late winter and early spring months when food availability begins to increase.

Longevity estimates for Lycodes squamiventer indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years], a figure derived from otolith increment analysis of individuals maintained at 0.9 °C [T = 0.9 °C]. This remarkable lifespan is considerably longer than the five years reported in earlier FishBase entries, reflecting recent revisions based on improved aging techniques. The extended longevity is consistent with the slow life-history pace observed in many deep-water and polar fish species, where low metabolic rates, delayed maturation, and reduced reproductive output combine to produce iteroparous adults that reproduce over many seasons. The presence of multiple age classes in trawl samples suggests that the population experiences relatively low natural mortality once individuals reach adult size. Senescence appears to be gradual, with older females retaining reproductive capability, albeit with diminished fecundity in the oldest age classes.

Additional comparative analysis of life-history traits within the genus Lycodes reveals that L. squamiventer falls at the slower end of the continuum. The ultimate total length of 26 cm [Li = 26 cm] places it among the smaller-bodied members of the genus, which includes species exceeding 60 cm in maximum length. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of 40 g [Wwi = 40 g] is modest relative to these larger congeners, yet the species achieves a comparable longevity to much larger-bodied zoarcids, suggesting that environmental temperature rather than body size per se is the primary determinant of lifespan in this group. The wet weight at birth of 0.0224 g [Wwb = 0.0224 g] is typical for the genus, reflecting a conserved egg size that balances provisioning against fecundity. Together, these measurements paint a portrait of a small, slow-growing, late-maturing fish that has evolved to persist in one of the most thermally stable and food-limited marine environments on Earth.
